Deep in the quarry sits a stone that thinks of a number from 1 to 100 and gives you five guesses. Write the game it plays.

Your program has three functions. The last lines, under `if __name__ == "__main__":`, start the game only when the whole program runs; the first two stages check your functions on their own. To make testing possible, the stone's secret number is the first line the program reads. In a real game you would let Python pick it: `import random`, then `random.randint(1, 100)` gives a whole number from 1 to 100.

Stage 1: `hint(secret, guess)` returns `"higher"` when the guess is too small, `"lower"` when it is too big, and `"correct"` when it is right.

Stage 2: `read_guess(text)` returns the guess as an int, ignoring spaces around it, or `None` when the text is not a whole number from 1 to 100. `None` is Python's value for "nothing".

Stage 3: `play(secret)` reads guesses with `input()` (no question text). For each guess it prints `higher` or `lower`, or `Correct! Guesses used: N` and stops. A line that is not a valid guess prints `Please type a whole number from 1 to 100.` and does not use up a guess. After 5 wrong guesses it prints `Out of guesses. It was SECRET.` Inside a loop, `continue` jumps straight to the next round and `return` leaves the function.

The marsh school's gradebook got soaked, and only its lines of text survived. Each line is a name, a colon, then marks separated by commas, like `Noa: 12, 15, 9`.

Write three functions in one program. Each stage checks one more of them; a beaten stage stays beaten.

Stage 1: `parse_line(line)` returns the name and a list of int marks: `parse_line("Noa: 12, 15, 9")` gives `("Noa", [12, 15, 9])`. A line with no marks, like `"Ines:"`, gives an empty list: `"".split(",")` is `[""]`, so skip empty pieces before calling `int()`. Split the line on `:` first and strip each piece, since `"Ines:".split(": ")` finds no `": "` at all.

Stage 2: `average(marks)` returns the mean of the marks rounded to 2 decimals. No marks gives `0.0`.

Stage 3: `ranking(lines)` returns `(name, average)` pairs, best average first. Equal averages are in alphabetical order. Blank lines (empty or only spaces) are skipped, and the list it is given stays as it was. Tip: `sorted(pairs, key=lambda pair: (-pair[1], pair[0]))` sorts by average, highest first, then by name. `lambda pair: ...` is a tiny one-line function, and the minus sign flips the order.

You left your satchel somewhere in the ruins. Write a tiny text adventure to go and get it back: rooms are a dict of dicts, commands come from `input()`, and what you pick up goes into a list.

The rooms are given in `ROOMS`. Each room has a `description`, its `exits` (a dict from direction to room name) and its `items` (a list). Four stages: read a command, move, pick things up, then the whole game.

Hard mode starts from an empty page, so here is the map to copy:

```python
ROOMS = {
    "gate": {"description": "A broken gate. A path leads north.", "exits": {"north": "hall"}, "items": []},
    "hall": {"description": "A hall of fallen pillars. Exits: south, east.", "exits": {"south": "gate", "east": "vault"}, "items": ["lamp"]},
    "vault": {"description": "A quiet vault. Your satchel lies here!", "exits": {"west": "hall"}, "items": ["satchel"]},
}
```

Stage 1: `parse(command)` returns a `(verb, noun)` pair in lower case, ignoring extra spaces: `parse("Take Lamp")` is `("take", "lamp")`, `parse("take old lamp")` is `("take", "old lamp")`, `parse("look")` is `("look", "")` and `parse("")` is `("", "")`.

Stage 2: `move(rooms, here, direction)` returns the room that exit leads to, or `here` when there is no exit that way.

Stage 3: `take(rooms, here, item, satchel)` moves `item` from the room's items into the `satchel` list and returns `True`. If the item is not in the room it changes nothing and returns `False`.

Stage 4: `play()` starts in `"gate"`, prints its description, then reads commands with `input()` until `quit` (print `Bye!`). `look` prints the description, then `You see: ...` if there are items. `go DIR` prints the new room's description, or `You can't go that way.`. `take ITEM` prints `Taken: ITEM` or `There is no ITEM here.`; taking the satchel prints `Taken: satchel`, then `You found the lost satchel. Well done!`, and ends the game. `inventory` prints `Satchel: lamp, map` or `Satchel: (empty)`. Anything else prints `I don't understand.`

The songbirds in the bramble maze keep forgetting their songs. Build them a playlist that behaves like one of Python's own containers: `len` works on it, `print` shows it nicely, and `in` finds a song.

Three stages: a `Song` dataclass, a `Playlist` class, then searching and sorting. Hard mode starts from an empty page.

Stage 1: Make `Song` a dataclass with fields `title` (str) and `seconds` (int), so `Song("Dawn", 90)` shows as `Song(title='Dawn', seconds=90)` and equals another `Song("Dawn", 90)`.

Stage 2: `Playlist(name)` keeps its own list of songs. `add(song)` adds one, `len(playlist)` counts them (write `__len__`), and `str(playlist)` is like `"Morning: 2 songs"` (write `__str__`).

Stage 3: `"Dawn" in playlist` should be `True` when a song has that title: write `__contains__(self, title)`, which `in` calls for you. `sorted_by_length()` returns the songs shortest first, using a key function; songs of equal length keep the order they were added in.

Ranger Noa keeps track of every animal in the forest, and the old den is full of loose papers. Build the ranger's registry with everything World 2 taught: classes, inheritance, composition, errors, and a test of your own.

Four stages: animals and birds, keepers, the registry itself, then a test that would catch a careless registry. Beat it, and the Ranger's Badge will get you over the rockslide to the mountains.

Stage 1: `Animal(name, species)` has `describe()` returning `"Sly the fox"`. `Bird(Animal)` also takes a `wingspan` and its `describe()` adds `", wingspan 95 cm"` to the animal's text. Remember `super().__init__(...)`.

Stage 2: `Keeper(name)` keeps its `name` and has its own list of animals: `adopt(animal)` adds one, and `feed_all()` returns `["Sly is fed", ...]` in adoption order.

Stage 3: `Registry()` starts with empty `animals` and `log` lists. `arrive(animal)` adds the animal and logs `"Sly arrived"`, but raises `ValueError("Sly is already registered")` when an animal with that name is already there. `find(name)` returns the animal with that name, or `None`. Keep the animals only in `self.animals`.

Stage 4: Write `test_registry()` with `assert`s: register an animal and find it, check that an unknown name gives `None`, and check that a second arrival with the same name raises `ValueError` (for example `assert False` right after the second `arrive`, inside a `try` that catches `ValueError`). It must pass on your registry and fail on a careless one that never refuses a name.

The old mine's shop sells lamps, ropes and picks to climbers, and writes every sale on a slip of CSV. Turn the slips into a report the miners can keep.

Three stages: read the sales, total them per product, then save the report as JSON and read it back. Hard mode starts from an empty page.

Stage 1: `read_sales(text)` reads CSV text with the columns `product`, `quantity` and `price`, and returns a list of dicts, one per row, like `{"product": "lamp", "quantity": 2, "price": 12.5}`. With pandas, `df.to_dict("records")` gives one dict per row. The quantity is a plain `int`, the price a plain `float` (convert with `int()` and `float()`). A price can have a thousands comma, in quotes like `"1,200"`: that is `1200.0`.

Stage 2: `totals(sales)` takes the list from `read_sales` and returns a dict of each product and the money it brought in (quantity times price, added up over all its rows).

Stage 3: `save_report(path, sales)` writes a JSON report to `path`: `{"total": ..., "by_product": totals(sales), "best": the product that brought in the most}`. With no sales, `total` is `0` and `best` is `None`. `load_report(path)` reads it back as a dict. `json.dump` refuses NumPy whole numbers (like `numpy.int64`) and NumPy `True`/`False`, so turn every number into a plain `int` or `float`.

The weather station on the windy ridge logs the wind every hour, and the wind gets into the log too: blank readings, words where numbers should be, hours written twice. Make sense of it.

Three stages: clean the readings, sum them up, then find the strongest gusts and count the hours over a limit. Hard mode starts from an empty page.

Stage 1: `clean(rows)` gets strings like `"06:00,12"` (an hour and a wind speed) and returns the speeds as plain floats, in order. Skip a row whose speed is blank or not a number (`float()` raises `ValueError` then), and when an hour comes twice, keep only its first usable reading.

Stage 2: `summary(speeds)` returns a dict with the `count`, the `mean` rounded to 2 decimals, the `median`, and the standard deviation `std` with `ddof=0` rounded to 2 decimals. Return plain numbers (`float()`), not NumPy ones. With no speeds, the `count` is `0` and the other three are `None`.

Stage 3: `top(speeds, n)` returns the `n` biggest speeds, biggest first. `count_over(speeds, limit)` returns how many speeds are above `limit` (a speed equal to the limit is not above it): sort them, then let `bisect` find where `limit` falls. `bisect.bisect_right` is like `bisect_left`, but gives the place just after any values equal to `limit`.

At the peak, the night is clear and the stars are many. Each one in the catalogue has a temperature (in kelvin) and a brightness, and Alex has labelled some: dwarf, sunlike or giant. Teach a program to label the rest.

Four stages: scale the features, find the nearest star by hand, let scikit-learn vote, then prove the model works on stars it has never seen. Hard mode starts from an empty page.

Stage 1: `scale_columns(rows)` takes a list of rows of numbers and returns new rows where each column is scaled to 0 to 1: `(value - smallest) / (largest - smallest)` within its column; a column where every value is the same scales to `0.0`. Temperatures in the thousands must not swamp brightness.

Stage 2: `nearest_label(X, y, point)` returns the label in `y` of the row of `X` nearest to `point`, by hand with `math.dist`.

Stage 3: `knn_predict(X, y, rows, k)` fits a scikit-learn `KNeighborsClassifier` with `k` neighbours on `X` and `y`, and returns a plain list of its labels for `rows`. If `k` is bigger than the number of known stars, raise your own `ValueError` with a message that mentions the stars (scikit-learn's error does not).

Stage 4: `star_accuracy(X, y)` scales `X` with your `scale_columns`, splits it with `test_size=0.25` and `random_state=0`, fits a 3-neighbour model on the training part, and returns its accuracy on the test part as a plain float. It must reach 0.8 (on this split, giving every star the same label scores 0.5 at best, and skipping the scaling scores 0.4). To keep it simple, the whole catalogue is scaled before the split; in real projects you scale with the training rows only, so the test rows stay unseen.
